Luminosity & vernier scans at sPHENIX

2023 – 2025 · Postdoctoral Researcher, CEA Paris-Saclay (DPhN) · sPHENIX at RHIC

Every cross-section a collider experiment publishes is divided by a luminosity. Somebody has to measure how hard the beams actually collide — and the naive Gaussian answer is not good enough.

What a vernier scan measures

The two beams are deliberately swept across each other while the collision rate is recorded. The rate as a function of separation traces out the beam-overlap integral; its width converts a raw counting rate into an absolute luminosity. Fit the scan, and you have calibrated your luminosity monitor for the whole run.

The complication is that a real machine is not two static Gaussians. Bunches cross at an angle, the transverse size grows away from the interaction point (the hourglass, or β*, effect), and the longitudinal profile is not a single Gaussian. Ignore these and the extracted width — and therefore the luminosity — is biased.

bunch-collider

So I wrote bunch-collider, a simulation of colliding relativistic bunches that models the scan properly and lets the beam parameters be constrained from the scan data itself.

  • Bunch model3D Gaussian, arbitrary z profile
  • Effectscrossing angle, hourglass β*
  • Longitudinalup to 4 Gaussians or tabulated PDF
  • Luminosityrelativistic Møller factor
  • CoreC++ via pybind11
  • Scalingtime steps across CPU cores

Other sPHENIX work

  • 2024 p+p run QA — tools to assess and validate data quality for the spin physics analyses.
  • DAQ monitoring — a GUI that alerts shift crews to beam losses and abnormal rates, cutting dead time and freeing the crew for other tasks.
  • Zero Degree Calorimeters — helped re-commission them for the polarized proton run, enabling verification of spin polarization at the collision point.
